title: Light - Reflection and Refraction
notes: Reflection of Light: The bouncing back of light when it hits a polished surface like a mirror.
Laws of Reflection: (i) Angle of incidence = Angle of reflection (angle i = angle r). (ii) The incident ray, reflected ray, and the normal all lie in the same plane.
Spherical Mirrors: Two types - Concave mirror (reflecting surface curves inward) and Convex mirror (reflecting surface curves outward).

Pole: Centre of the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror. Centre of Curvature: Centre of the sphere of which the mirror is a part. Principal Axis: The line joining the Pole (P) and Centre of Curvature (C). Radius of Curvature: The distance PC. The principal axis is normal to the mirror at the pole.

Principal Focus (F) and Focal Length (f): For a concave mirror, parallel rays converge at the focus (converging mirror). For a convex mirror, parallel rays appear to diverge from the focus (diverging mirror). In our syllabus, Radius of curvature R = 2f.
Image formation: If rays of light actually meet, the image is Real. If rays of light appear to meet, the image is Virtual.

Uses of Concave Mirror: Used in torches, search lights and vehicle headlights to get powerful parallel beams; used by dentists to see large images of teeth; concave mirrors are used in solar furnaces (concentrating sunlight to a point).
Uses of Convex Mirror: Used as rear-view mirrors in vehicles because they give an upright/erect image and a wider field of view.

Sign Convention for spherical mirrors: (i) All distances are measured from the pole. (ii) Distances measured in the direction of the incident ray are positive, and against it are negative. (iii) Heights measured upward are positive, heights measured downward are negative.
Mirror Formula: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u, where f = focal length, v = image distance, u = object distance.
Magnification (mirror): m = h'/h = -v/u, where h' = height of image, h = height of object.
Note: u is negative for real objects (in front of mirror), v is negative for real images, positive for virtual images.
Spherical Lenses: Convex lens (thick in the middle) converges light rays. Concave lens (thin in the middle) diverges light rays. Principal axis and optical centre are the reference lines/points.
Principal Focus (F) and Focal Length (f) for lenses: Convex lens has two foci F1 and F2 due to two curved surfaces (converging lens). Concave lens also has two foci F1 and F2 (diverging lens).

Image formation by convex lens: Object at infinity gives a real, inverted, highly diminished, point-sized image at F2. Object beyond 2F1 gives a real, inverted, diminished image between F2 and 2F2. Object at 2F1 gives a real, inverted, same-size image at 2F2. Object between F1 and 2F1 gives a real, inverted, enlarged image beyond 2F2. Object at F1 gives a real, inverted, highly enlarged image at infinity. Object between focus and optical centre gives a virtual, erect, enlarged image on the same side as the object.

Image formation by concave lens: For an object at any finite distance, the image is virtual, erect, diminished, and located between the optical centre and F1. For an object at infinity, the image is virtual, erect, highly diminished (point-sized) at the focus.
Summary - Convex lens: Inverted, exact/upright, magnified image (except when object is between optical centre and F, gives erect, magnified virtual image).
Summary - Concave lens: Always gives an erect, upright, diminished virtual image regardless of object position.
Sign Convention, Lens Formula and Magnification: All distances are measured from the optical centre (O). Same rules for sign as mirrors apply otherwise.
Lens Formula: 1/f = 1/v - 1/u.
Magnification (lens): m = h'/h = v/u.
Sign convention values: u is always negative, f is positive for a convex lens and negative for a concave lens.

Power of a Lens: Ability of a lens to converge or diverge rays of light. Defined as the reciprocal of focal length. P = 1/f (f in metres). Unit of power is Dioptre (D). Convex lens has positive power, concave lens has negative power.
Power of combination of lenses: P = P1 + P2 + P3 + ... (total power equals sum of individual powers, when lenses are placed in contact).
Refraction of Light: The bending of a light ray when it travels from one medium to another.

When light travels from a rarer medium to a denser medium, it bends towards the normal. When light travels from a denser medium to a rarer medium, it bends away from the normal. When there is no change of medium, there is no bending.
Refractive Index (R.I.): A measure of how dense a medium is. n21 = n2/n1 = v1/v2, where v1 and v2 are the speeds of light in medium 1 and medium 2 respectively.
R.I. of medium 2 with respect to medium 1: n21 = n2/n1 = v1/v2. Also n21 = v1/v2 and n12 = n1/n2 = v2/v1.
Absolute Refractive Index: When the first medium is air and the second medium is any medium x. nwa (or nx) = n(medium)/n(air) = v(air)/v(medium). Taking n(air) = 1 and v(air) = c: nx = c/vx.
R.I. of glass is 1.5. R.I. of water is 1.33.
Which is more dense (optically)? Glass. In which medium does light travel faster? Water.

Refraction Through a Glass Slab: Light bends towards the normal when entering the denser glass (air to glass), and bends away from the normal when exiting back into air (glass to air). The emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray. Angle of emergence (angle e) = Angle of incidence (angle i).

Laws of Refraction: (i) The incident ray, refracted ray, and normal all lie on the same plane. (ii) The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction remains constant for a given pair of media (Snell's Law).
Snell's Law: sin(i)/sin(r) = constant = n21 = n2/n1.

Cases of No Bending: (1) Normal incidence - when light hits the boundary perpendicular to the surface (angle of incidence = 0), there is no refraction/bending. (2) No medium change / no change in refractive index - if angle i = angle r = 0.

examples.question: State the uses of a concave mirror.
examples.solution: Concave mirrors are used in torches, search lights and vehicle headlights to get powerful parallel beams of light, by dentists to see enlarged images of teeth, and in solar furnaces to concentrate sunlight to a point.

examples.question: What is the nature of image formed by a convex lens when the object is between the optical centre and focus, versus a concave lens for any object position?
examples.solution: For a convex lens with the object between the optical centre and F, the image is virtual, erect, and enlarged, on the same side as the object. For a concave lens, regardless of object position, the image is always virtual, erect, and diminished.

examples.question: Why does a light ray bend towards the normal when going from air to glass, but there is no bending at normal incidence?
examples.solution: Light bends towards the normal when passing from a rarer medium (air) to a denser medium (glass) because its speed decreases. At normal incidence, the angle of incidence is 0 degrees, so there is no bending even though the medium changes.
